Title: 9 Templates for Responding to Complaints on Your Social Channels | Likeable
# 9 Templates for Responding to Complaints on Your Social Channels. Social media is a great tool for creating conversations with your audience—but it also opens a direct line of communication for complaints. These days, it isn’t an option for brands to respond to their customers on social; it’s expected. To get started, set up your brand’s support account bio to include on-duty hours, a dedicated email address for inquiries, and the languages you support. Once you’ve done that, you’re ready to respond. But remember: When it comes to complaints, there are levels of severity, each of which should be handled strategically. Here we’ve broken them down into Green (low-risk), Yellow (moderate-risk), and Red (high-risk). A “green tier” complaint is something that doesn’t pose an immediate threat to your brand’s customers, employees, or reputation. results.content:
## The main types of customer complaints

Before the examples, it helps to know the 3 broad buckets most complaints fall into. Sorting a complaint into one of these tells you who needs to be involved in the fix:

 Product-related: The product is defective, low quality, missing a feature, or does not match what was advertised. These often need your product or engineering team.
 Service or people-related: A rude agent, a long hold, or an unhelpful interaction. These are about how your team treats customers and are usually fixed through training and staffing.
 Process-related: Confusing policies, repeated information requests, or clunky checkout and delivery flows. These are friction points baked into how your business runs. [...] ## What are customer complaints?

A customer complaint is any expression of dissatisfaction with your product, service, or support experience. It can arrive privately through an email, a support ticket, or a survey, or publicly through a review site or social media.

Complaints feel like setbacks, but they are really free diagnostics. Each one points to a gap between what a customer expected and what they got. Ignore them and you lose customers quietly. Act on them and you get a clear roadmap for what to improve.

The stakes are high. With nearly a third of customers willing to walk away from a brand they love after a single bad experience, one unhandled complaint can be the difference between a loyal customer and a lost one.
